topic: Clock escapements and the mechanics of ticking
stimulus:
A clock doesn't really measure time; it counts the stutters of a thing that wants to unwind. The mainspring pushes, and the escapement says no, not yet, then yes, a little. That tick is a tiny act of rationing. The anchor escapement rocks back and forth, catching teeth on a wheel, and the sound is the wheel slamming into a brake over and over. Time as a controlled series of collisions.

Which makes me think of pendulums, and Galileo supposedly watching a swinging lamp in Pisa, though that story smells embroidered. Anyway, a pendulum's period depends on length, not weight, so a clock runs slow in summer when the brass rod expands. Hence Harrison's gridiron pendulum, bars of two metals fighting each other's expansion so the net length stays put. Cancellation as craftsmanship.

Then there's the longitude problem, where a wobbly ship made pendulums useless, so he built springs and balance wheels that ignored gravity's direction. Sailors' lives hung on a watch not noticing the sea.

Quartz does the same job with a vibrating crystal at 32,768 hertz, a number chosen because it's two to the fifteenth, so fifteen halvings give one pulse per second. Binary hiding inside your wristwatch. Meanwhile atomic clocks count cesium's jitter, and the second is officially a pile of 9,192,631,770 cycles. Oddly specific, like a phone number for eternity.

A Fresnel lens looks like a dinner plate that gave up being thick. Augustin Fresnel noticed that bending light happens at the surface, so the glass in the middle is mostly dead weight. Slice it into concentric rings, keep only the angled faces, and you get the same focus with a fraction of the mass. Same trick lives in overhead projectors and the little plastic magnifier cards people keep in wallets.

Before that, lighthouses burned coal fires on hilltops, then oil lamps backed by polished reflectors, which wasted most of the light. The lens caught what escaped sideways and bent it into a beam. Some lenses floated on a trough of liquid mercury so a keeper could turn a multi-ton assembly with a fingertip. Mercury, strange heavy mirror-metal, doing bearing duty. Keepers wound clockwork weights like grandfather clocks, climbing stairs every few hours to keep the beam turning.

The flash pattern is the fingerprint: two seconds on, six off, or group-flashing three. Sailors identify a headland by counting. A lighthouse is basically a slow, analog Morse transmitter that only says "here."

Fog complicates things. Light dies, so horns and bells took over, and sound carries oddly, sometimes skipping over silent zones where the horn can't be heard at all.

Now GPS makes most of it ceremonial. Yet the towers stay, painted in stripes so daytime sailors can tell them apart too.

A Fresnel lens looks like a glass beehive, concentric rings stacked like a cake sliced thin. The trick is that you only need the curved surface of a lens, not its bulk, so Fresnel collapsed the thick middle into steps. Weight drops, light still bends. Funny that the same idea now sits in cheap plastic sheets for magnifying page corners and in car backup-camera stickers.

Lighthouses were once tended by keepers who wound clockwork like grandfather clocks, with weights descending through the tower's hollow core. Some floated the whole lens assembly in a bath of mercury so one finger could spin a several-ton apparatus. Mercury fumes probably explain a few stories of keepers going strange, though I'm wary of tidy explanations.

Each lighthouse has a "characteristic": two flashes every ten seconds, or one long and one short. It's basically Morse code as identity, a fingerprint at sea. Sailors compared the pattern against a chart, which is a kind of lookup table made of photons.

Then there's the paint. Daymarks, the stripes and spirals, exist because the light is useless at noon. Cape Hatteras has its barber-pole spiral; others are checkered. Same building, two shifts, two signaling systems. Meanwhile GPS made most of this ornamental, yet the beams still turn, humming faintly, in places nobody visits.

A Fresnel lens is a strange thing: take a thick glass lens, slice it into concentric rings, throw away the bulky middle of each slice, and keep only the curved surface that bends light. Same focusing, a fraction of the glass. Augustin Fresnel did this in the 1820s, and suddenly a lighthouse beam could reach twenty miles instead of five. Before that, people burned coal fires on hilltops, which is a lovely, smoky way to say "rocks here."

The lens floated on a bath of mercury in some towers, so one keeper could rotate tons of glass with a gentle push. Mercury, of all things, as a bearing. Clockwork weights hung down the tower's core and had to be wound every few hours, which is why lighthouse stairs spiral: they wrap around a falling weight.

Each lighthouse has a signature, a "characteristic": two flashes every ten seconds, or long-short-long. A navigator's night sky made of fixed patterns, like constellations that someone commissioned. Meanwhile the modern LED beacon has no moving parts and fits in a bucket, and old lenses end up in museums or in a rich person's garden, catching rain instead of ships.

Which reminds me of the Fresnel rings in old overhead projectors, those faint grooves on the glass, and car-rear-window magnifiers stuck on with static.

A Fresnel lens looks like a dinner plate that gave up being thick. Augustin Fresnel noticed that only the surface of a lens bends light; the glass in the middle just sits there being heavy. So he sliced the curve into concentric rings and threw the bulk away. Suddenly a lens taller than a person could be built from prisms stacked like a beehive, and a lamp's glow could reach twenty miles. Funny that the same trick shows up in overhead projectors, car taillights, and those flimsy plastic magnifiers tucked in wallets.

The rotation is the part I like. The beam isn't a pulse at all; the lens just sweeps a steady beam past you, and your eye turns it into a flash. Each lighthouse has its own rhythm, two long, one short, a pause, so sailors can identify it like a name. Characters in the dark, written in time rather than ink.

The lens floated on a bath of liquid mercury so a clockwork weight could spin tons of glass with a nudge. Keepers wound it by hand, trimmed wicks, polished brass. Mercury fumes are a whole other story. Then automation arrived, LEDs and GPS, and the keepers left. Meanwhile, the lenses are sold at auction, sitting in museum lobbies, still quietly bending nothing at all.

Bridges are strange because they're mostly about not moving, and yet the famous ones are remembered for moving. Tacoma Narrows, 1940, twisting itself apart in a wind that wasn't even strong. Everyone says resonance, but the textbook story is slightly wrong: it was aeroelastic flutter, the bridge feeding on the wind's energy the way a reed feeds on breath in a clarinet. A bridge as a very slow, very large woodwind.

Soldiers break step crossing bridges, an old rule, and the Millennium Bridge in London wobbled in 2000 because walkers unconsciously synchronized with the sway, each step nudging the next. Nobody planned it. Crowds tune themselves, like fireflies or applauding audiences drifting into rhythm.

Suspension cables are really just chains hung under gravity, and a hanging chain makes a catenary, which Gaudí flipped upside down to design arches. Model it in string and weights, then invert the photograph. Cathedral from dangling rope.

Then there's the expansion joint, those metal teeth in the road you thump over. Steel grows in summer heat, so the bridge needs gaps to breathe. The Golden Gate rises and falls several feet over a day. Painters there supposedly never finish; rust catches up. Which loops back to Tacoma, and to paint, and to Venice's wooden pilings, which are really petrified under water, hardly rotting at all.

A Fresnel lens is a strange thing: take a thick curved glass lens, slice it into concentric rings, throw away the bulky middle of each slice, and keep only the surface curvature. The bending of light survives the diet. Augustin Fresnel did this in the 1820s, and suddenly a lamp could be seen twenty miles out to sea. Before that, lighthouses used mirrors that lost most of the light to tarnish and soot.

The lens floats in a bath of mercury in many old towers, so a multi-ton assembly of brass and glass can spin with a nudge from a clockwork weight. Keepers wound that clockwork by hand, like feeding a very large cuckoo clock. Mercury, of course, is a nasty neighbor, and some keepers reportedly went strange, though that's a story I half remember rather than something I'd bet on.

The flash patterns are an alphabet: two seconds on, six off, identifies a particular rock. Each light has a signature, like a bird call or a Morse name. Daytime paint stripes do the same job, black spirals, red bands.

Then GPS arrived and the whole apparatus became charming rather than necessary. Yet theatre spotlights and car headlights borrowed the ridged trick, and so did the thin plastic magnifier sheets that sit in wallets. Overhead projectors too, those humming classroom machines with their warm glass tops and smudged transparencies.

A Fresnel lens is a strange thing: take a thick curved lens, slice it into concentric rings, throw away the bulk glass that only carried light along without bending it, and keep just the surfaces that do the bending. Weight collapses, yet the beam survives. Augustin Fresnel did this in the 1820s, and suddenly a lighthouse could throw light twenty miles without a lens the size of a boulder. Now the same trick lives in cheap plastic sheets sold for reading maps, and in the stepped glass of old traffic signals, and in the ridged faces of stage spotlights.

The rotating lenses floated on a bath of mercury, which is odd enough: a multi-ton assembly of brass and glass turned by a finger's push because liquid metal has almost no friction. Keepers wound clockwork weights like grandfather clocks, climbing stairs every few hours. The flash patterns were signatures, like Morse for geography: two seconds on, six off, meaning this rock and not that one. A sailor's chart was a list of rhythms.

Which makes me think of fog signals, horns pitched low because low sound travels farther, and of how sound sometimes skips over silent zones where the horn can't be heard at all. Then radar beacons, then GPS, and the quiet retirement of towers into wedding venues and postage stamps.
